evals.prompt:
Can you turn this conversation into an HTML report that I can share with my team? They weren't part of the discussion and I want them to understand the different ways OTT platforms work together.

Conversation:
Q: I searched 'Weapons' in Apple TV, it showed it's on Prime, and there's a direct open option. How does this cross-platform search work?
A: This is called universal search. Apple runs a content metadata aggregation layer where streaming services register their catalogs. Prime Video, Disney+, etc submit their full content libraries to Apple using the TV App Provider framework. Apple indexes all of this centrally. When you search, Apple searches its own index - not Prime's servers in real time. The match is found, Apple already knows the deep link URI (like aiv://aiv/resume?...) to open that title directly in Prime. On other platforms: Android TV uses the Watch Next API, Roku has the Roku Search Partner Program.

Q: On Prime I can access Paramount content directly inside Prime. Does that mean Prime is connecting to Paramount servers, or is the video hosted on Prime servers? I'm watching Matlock which required a Paramount subscription.
A: This is Prime Video Channels. Amazon acts as a distribution marketplace. You subscribe to Paramount+ through Amazon (not directly). Two hosting models: (1) Paramount serves the video - Prime's player is just a shell, when you hit play it gets a stream URL from Paramount's CDN. (2) Amazon re-hosts the content - Paramount delivers files to Amazon's CloudFront CDN, Amazon serves the bytes. For major channels the second is more common now. Revenue split: Amazon takes 20-30%, Paramount gets 70-80%. DRM is key: even if Amazon hosts the file, Paramount's DRM servers (Widevine on Android, FairPlay on Apple) issue every playback license. So Amazon can host the file but Paramount controls who can play it.

Q: I subscribed to Spotify student which gives Hulu with ads. In Hulu I can access FX on Hulu, ABC, Hotstar, Fox. How does this work?
A: Three different models stacked. Layer 1: Spotify-Hulu bundle - pure marketing partnership, no technical integration. Layer 2: The hubs - Disney owns Hulu AND FX Networks (acquired via 21st Century Fox deal 2019), ABC (long-time Disney property), and Disney+ Hotstar. So FX, ABC, Hotstar on Hulu are all Disney properties - one company organizing its own content under branded labels. All served from Hulu's CDN. Fox is the exception: Fox was a founding Hulu partner in 2007, sold its stake to Disney but retained long-term content licensing agreements. General pattern: the more a platform owns its content partners, the simpler the technical and business plumbing.
evals.expected_output: A self-contained HTML file with dark header, TL;DR section, background context, organized sections explaining universal search/channels/hubs to someone unfamiliar, and a key takeaway. No assumption of prior knowledge.

evals.prompt:
Write this up as a shareable article - I want someone who knows nothing about streaming to be able to read this and understand how different platforms handle content from other services.

Source material:
- When you search a show on Apple TV and it says 'Available on Prime', Apple is searching its own pre-built index of Prime's catalog (not calling Prime in real time). Deep links fire to open the right app.
- Prime Video Channels lets you subscribe to Paramount+, Starz, etc through Amazon. Amazon often re-hosts the video files on its CDN but the content owner's DRM server still issues every playback key.
- Hulu hubs (FX on Hulu, ABC on Hulu, Hotstar on Hulu) are mostly Disney-owned properties shown under branded labels. Disney owns Hulu, FX, ABC, and Hotstar. Fox on Hulu exists because Fox was a founding Hulu partner who retained licensing rights after selling its equity stake.
- The more ownership overlap between platforms, the simpler the architecture. Universal search = no content moves. Channels = cross-company with DRM coordination. Owned hubs = internal reorganization.
evals.expected_output: A clean, readable HTML article for a streaming newcomer. Explains what DRM is, what a CDN is, what a 'channel marketplace' means, etc. Should feel like a journalist wrote it, not like a technical doc.
